items.title: What is the risk of PH in pregnancy?
items.q: What is the risk of PH in pregnancy?
items.a:
- PAH is mWHO IV/very high pregnancy risk; ESC 2025 cites contemporary mortality 11–25% with major phenotype/RV variation.
- Most deaths occur after delivery; high risk can persist for months. MDT counselling and an expert-centre delivery plan are essential.
- Avoid ERAs, riociguat and selexipag during pregnancy; use specialist pregnancy-compatible PAH therapy. Anticoagulation is indication-specific.
### Preop

- optimise and plan.

### Intraop

- controlled delivery, titrated neuraxial where suitable, cautious uterotonics.

### Postop

- ICU/specialist follow-up and continued therapy.

> **Closing point:** PAH requires explicit pregnancy counselling and prolonged postpartum planning.

Source: BJA Educ 2022

items.title: 1. Pulmonary arterial hypertension in late pregnancy: delivery
items.q: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks with pulmonary arterial hypertension is to be delivered. Discuss the risks and your anaesthetic plan.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Pulmonary arterial hypertension in pregnancy" (2023 issue; online 2022). **Blue Book:** Smith (2015); Toon, Graydon (2021).

### Risks

PAH is a **very high-risk pregnancy condition (mWHO IV)**, requiring explicit counselling against pregnancy and shared decision-making; not only severe pressure elevation carries risk. ESC 2025 reports contemporary maternal mortality **11–25%** across cited series, with marked variation by phenotype and RV status and highest in the **first weeks after delivery**. Physiology works against the RV: blood volume rises 40 to 50%, cardiac output rises, SVR falls, hypercoagulability, and the peripartum period brings autotransfusion with uterine contraction, pain, bleeding and fluid shifts.

### Preop — planning

- Multidisciplinary team (obstetrics, PH cardiology, anaesthesia, ICU) at a **tertiary centre**; individualised mode/timing of delivery, often a planned caesarean for controlled conditions, with a written haemodynamic/haemorrhage/rescue plan. **34–36 weeks is not a mandatory target**; at 36 weeks assess maternal trajectory and fetal factors without harmful delay. Continue PAH therapy (sildenafil, inhaled or IV prostanoids); avoid **endothelin receptor antagonists, riociguat and selexipag** during pregnancy per ESC 2025; avoid sotatercept because of fetal harm risk. Anticoagulation is indication-specific, not automatic for every PAH patient; when required, coordinate LMWH interruption (therapeutic dosing generally ≥24 hours before planned delivery/neuraxial intervention) and local neuraxial guidance.
- Pre-op echo, BNP, risk stratification, arterial line, and a plan for ICU or HDU for at least 48 to 72 hours.

### Intraop — delivery and anaesthesia

- **Aim:** maintain SVR and RV coronary perfusion, avoid increases in PVR, and keep preload.
- **Neuraxial:** a slowly titrated **epidural or combined spinal-epidural** (or low-dose, slow CSE) is favoured; single-shot spinal causes abrupt SVR fall and is avoided. GA reserved for emergencies or contraindications, but is high risk (induction hypotension, positive pressure ventilation).
- Arterial line before; central line with caution; avoid PAC.
- **Drugs:** vasopressor (phenylephrine or noradrenaline) ready; **avoid ergometrine and carboprost** (raise PVR); give oxytocin slowly in small boluses or an infusion (it lowers SVR and raises PVR). Consider **inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin** in the theatre.
- Tranexamic acid, cell salvage, and avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, pain and shivering.

### Postop — postpartum

ICU monitoring during delivery and postpartum, with duration individualised; **risk persists for many weeks to months**, so discharge at 72 hours does not end surveillance. [ESC pregnancy 2025][PREG] continue PAH therapy; thromboprophylaxis; avoid fluid overload; contraception and counselling.

**Key evidence:** [BJAPREG][BJAPREG] · [PREG][PREG] · [PH][PH]

### An antenatal-to-postpartum plan, not a delivery-only answer

At 36 weeks, establish the woman's trajectory and current RV reserve urgently: symptoms, syncope, functional class, saturation, congestion, ECG, biomarkers and serial specialist echo. Review whether maternal deterioration changes timing or location of delivery. Discuss prematurity and neonatal support, maternal wishes and the limitations of available outcome estimates; historical mortality rates are not an individual prediction. Prepare a written plan for spontaneous labour, urgent caesarean and failed neuraxial analgesia as well as the intended delivery. Anticoagulation timing must permit the chosen technique and protect against bleeding. Continue pregnancy-compatible PAH therapy with backup delivery arrangements and avoid fetal-harm agents. After delivery, do not interpret successful extubation as the end of risk: autotransfusion, fluid mobilisation, haemorrhage, thrombosis and arrhythmia can destabilise the RV. Arrange specialist critical care and follow-up beyond the first postoperative day.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains why pregnancy and the postpartum period are high risk
- Plans MDT and delivery timing; continues PAH therapy and avoids teratogens
- Chooses a titrated neuraxial technique and avoids single-shot spinal
- Arterial line and cautious central access
- Avoids ergometrine and carboprost and gives oxytocin cautiously
- Prepares inhaled pulmonary vasodilators and vasopressors
- Plans ICU care and contraception

items.title: 2025.2 Q4: Discuss the antenatal anaesthesia assessment and planning for a G1P0 p
items.q: Discuss the antenatal anaesthesia assessment and planning for a G1P0 pregnant patient at 24 weeks gestation with moderate idiopathic pulmonary hypertension.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus:** High maternal/fetal risk; antenatal assessment, serial review and medical optimisation; compare GA and neuraxial options. The report specifically criticises answers restricted to pregnancy physiology or delivery alone. Named PH overlap in the Set 12 master; general obstetric care remains in the obstetric sets.

### Recognise risk and arrange the team

This is a **24-week antenatal consultation**, not an immediate caesarean. PAH is a very high-risk pregnancy (mWHO IV); a label of “moderate” pressure does not establish moderate overall risk. Maternal RV failure, arrhythmia, thrombosis/bleeding and death, and fetal loss, prematurity and growth restriction require sensitive counselling with the Pregnancy Heart Team. Establish the woman's wishes, existing advice and access to specialist care; discuss all pregnancy options within specialist/local practice without treating risk classification as a decision made for her.

### Assess the woman and her trajectory

Clarify the actual diagnosis, WHO group and cause, previous decompensation, hospitalisations, syncope, chest pain, functional class, exercise tolerance and change during pregnancy. Review signs of RV failure, resting/exertional oxygenation, BP, rhythm, congestion and associated disease. Obtain original RHC data—mPAP, PAWP, PVR, RAP and cardiac index—and recent specialist echo for RV size/function, septal position, TR, pericardial effusion and LV function. Use serial echo, symptoms and biomarkers as clinically indicated; do not repeat RHC automatically merely to obtain a new pressure. Review Hb/iron, platelets, renal/liver function, ECG, BNP/NT-proBNP, medication adherence and oxygen requirements. Assess airway, obesity/OSA, reflux, prior anaesthesia, neuraxial feasibility and anticoagulant timing.

Review fetal growth/wellbeing and obstetric factors with maternal-fetal medicine. A clear follow-up schedule, deterioration criteria and contact pathway are essential because risk changes with gestation.

### Optimise and plan before delivery

Continue **pregnancy-compatible PAH therapy** under the PH team, often PDE5/prostacyclin pathway treatment according to severity. Endothelin receptor antagonists, riociguat and other fetal-harm agents require specialist withdrawal/substitution; never abruptly interrupt a necessary prostacyclin infusion. Sotatercept is not a pregnancy rescue treatment. Individualise oxygen, cautious diuresis, rhythm management and anticoagulation: neither therapeutic anticoagulation nor fluid loading is automatic in every PAH pregnancy. Arrange dedicated infusion access, backup supplies and trained staff if an infusion is used.

Agree the specialist delivery centre, likely timing/mode, anaesthetist/ICU/neonatal involvement, resources for inhaled vasodilators and rescue support, and plans for spontaneous labour, urgent caesarean and maternal collapse. Mode and timing depend on maternal RV status, obstetric considerations and team experience; do not impose the same week or caesarean on every patient.

### Compare anaesthetic options

A **carefully titrated epidural or selected low-dose sequential technique** can limit pain, catecholamine surges and positive-pressure ventilation, but abrupt sympathectomy may collapse SVR and right-coronary perfusion. Coagulation/anticoagulant timing and the possibility of an urgent operation must be addressed. A conventional rapid-onset single-shot spinal is generally avoided in significant PAH.

**GA** may be necessary for urgency, contraindicated/failed neuraxial or severe compromise. Risks include induction hypotension, difficult/aspiration-risk airway, sympathetic stimulation and the effects of positive pressure on venous return/PVR. Prepare an arterial line, haemodynamic support, careful induction and ventilation; it is not enough to say “GA is contraindicated.” No observational mortality comparison proves the technique alone caused the outcome.

### Postpartum planning begins now

Plan specialist critical care, cautious uterotonics and fluid/blood management, analgesia without hypoventilation, uninterrupted PAH therapy and surveillance during postpartum autotransfusion/fluid mobilisation. Risk extends beyond the first 24–48 h and may persist for weeks. Include counselling about contraception and future pregnancy, follow-up and psychological support. [PREG][PREG]

Assesses at 24 weeks with symptoms, RV function, serial review and investigations
Plans Pregnancy Heart Team and fetal assessment
Optimises pregnancy-compatible drugs and avoids unsafe interruption/teratogens
Compares benefits and hazards of both neuraxial and GA
Individualises delivery location, timing, mode and emergencies
Plans haemodynamic/respiratory support and appropriate monitoring
Includes postpartum surveillance and longer-term counselling

items.title: 2019.1 Q12: A 30-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant has been referred to your
items.q: A 30-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant has been referred to your tertiary high-risk obstetric clinic. She has complex cyanotic heart disease and now functions with a Fontan circulation. How would you stratify her cardiovascular risk? (30%) What are the relevant anaesthetic issues for this patient? (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus:** Stratify risk and provide tertiary MDT care; better answers distinguish labour, vaginal/operative delivery, blood loss and immediate postpartum issues. This is a congenital/shunt physiology overlap with obstetrics.

### Cardiovascular risk stratification (30%)

A Fontan is a palliated single-ventricle circulation: systemic venous return reaches the pulmonary arteries **without a subpulmonary pump**. Pulmonary flow and ventricular preload depend on adequate venous return, low PVR and a favourable transpulmonary gradient. Pregnancy increases volume/output demand and reduces reserve. This woman is already described as **cyanotic**, so quantify her baseline oxygenation and look for a fenestration, collaterals, baffle/conduit obstruction or failing Fontan rather than assuming uncomplicated physiology.

Review NYHA class and exercise tolerance, syncope, heart failure, prior arrhythmia/thrombosis, previous pregnancy/cardiac events and medication. Assess ventricular function, AV-valve regurgitation, Fontan pathway/pressures, rhythm and oxygenation with specialist echo and existing CMR/catheter data. Check Hb/iron, platelets, renal/liver function, coagulation, albumin/protein-losing enteropathy and signs of Fontan-associated liver disease. Consider maternal and fetal effects of cyanosis and low output. Use a pregnancy-specific framework such as **mWHO 2.0**, with a prediction tool as an adjunct rather than substituting for physiology. An uncomplicated well-functioning Fontan can be mWHO III; cyanosis, poor function, arrhythmia or Fontan complications can make pregnancy mWHO IV. Do not assign every Fontan the same class without assessing these features.

### Antenatal and delivery issues (70%)

Arrange a Pregnancy Heart Team including ACHD cardiology, obstetric anaesthesia, maternal-fetal medicine, ICU and neonatology. Review serial clinical status, saturation, echo and fetal growth; provide explicit triggers for urgent review. Counsel about heart failure, arrhythmia, thrombosis/paradoxical embolism, bleeding, fetal loss/growth restriction and prematurity. Plan at a centre with relevant expertise and rescue resources, with written pathways for spontaneous labour, urgent caesarean and decompensation.

Maintain effective preload without indiscriminate loading, low PVR, sinus rhythm/AV synchrony and adequate systemic perfusion. Avoid hypoxaemia, hypercarbia, acidosis, high mean airway pressure, pain and tachycardia. Anticoagulation/antiplatelet choice depends on prior thrombosis, arrhythmia, Fontan features and bleeding; coordinate neuraxial and delivery timing rather than routinely bridge everyone. De-air IV lines and use compatible filters, particularly with a fenestration/right-to-left pathway. Central access needs knowledge of Glenn/Fontan anatomy and venous obstruction.

### Labour, operative delivery and the postpartum period

Mode of delivery is individualised. A stable patient may tolerate vaginal delivery with **early carefully titrated epidural analgesia**, limiting pain and prolonged Valsalva with an assisted second stage when indicated. A caesarean may be needed for obstetric reasons or significant maternal compromise. Avoid abrupt neuraxial sympathectomy; GA carries induction/airway and positive-pressure risks and must be planned as an alternative or rescue. Anticoagulation/coagulopathy can preclude neuraxial anaesthesia. Use invasive monitoring according to severity, not a routine PAC in distorted venous anatomy.

Prepare for blood loss and cautious uterotonics; avoid abrupt hypotension or rises in PVR. Autotransfusion at uterine contraction and postpartum fluid mobilisation can overload a limited Fontan, while haemorrhage reduces passive pulmonary flow: manage both extremes promptly. Positive pressure may be necessary but use the lowest effective mean airway pressure, enough recruitment and controlled CO2; effective spontaneous ventilation helps only if gas exchange remains adequate.

Postpartum specialist monitoring must continue through fluid shifts, with careful balance, rhythm surveillance, analgesia, thromboprophylaxis/anticoagulation and resumption of drugs. Provide longer-term ACHD review and contraception counselling. A good immediate delivery outcome does not remove delayed heart-failure/thrombotic risk. [BB21][BB21] [PREG][PREG]
rubric: Explains passive Fontan flow and pregnancy consequences
Uses functional status, cyanosis, ventricular/valve function and previous events for risk
Distinguishes uncomplicated from complicated Fontan/mWHO categories
Includes antenatal specialist and fetal assessment
Plans both vaginal and operative delivery with analgesia/anaesthetic alternatives
Protects preload, PVR, perfusion, rhythm and air safety
Coordinates anticoagulation and neuraxial timing
Addresses haemorrhage, autotransfusion and delayed postpartum complications

items.title: 2. Rheumatic mitral stenosis and pulmonary hypertension in pregnancy
items.q: A 28-year-old woman at 34 weeks has rheumatic mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension. Discuss her risk and your plan for delivery and anaesthesia.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2023, "Obstetric anaesthesia in rheumatic heart disease" (Jhummon-Mahadnac et al).

### Why this is dangerous

Pregnancy raises cardiac output (about 40 to 50%) and heart rate, and labour adds pain-driven tachycardia and an autotransfusion after delivery. In mitral stenosis, tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, raising left atrial pressure and causing **pulmonary oedema** or AF. The hypercoagulable state also risks pulmonary embolism, which can precipitate acute RV failure.

### Risk stratification

Use current mWHO 2.0 classification and pregnancy-heart-team assessment. Severe MS, pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction raise risk; do not apply historical 30–56% PAH mortality to every patient with MS-associated postcapillary PH.

### Delivery planning

- Without an obstetric indication, **vaginal delivery** is preferred (less haemorrhage, infection and thromboembolism).
- mWHO II: spontaneous labour is reasonable if the patient lives close to the hospital.
- mWHO III and IV: **planned delivery in an expert centre with appropriate monitoring, sometimes ICU depending on severity; not obligatory ICU induction for every mWHO III/IV patient**, allowing continuous monitoring and optimisation of volume, rate control and anticoagulation before neuraxial block. Planned caesarean can suit the highest-risk patients.
- Consider cultural and social factors: relocating remote women near term removes support at a stressful time.

### Intraop

### Anaesthetic aims in mitral stenosis

- Keep the heart rate slow and sinus rhythm; treat AF promptly.
- Early, **slowly titrated epidural analgesia** to blunt the pain response; avoid abrupt falls in SVR.
- Maintain preload without volume overload; avoid anything that raises PVR (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis).
- Vasopressors: phenylephrine or metaraminol rather than ephedrine.
- Anticoagulation: check timing before neuraxial block.
- Prosthetic valves: bioprosthetic valves avoid therapeutic anticoagulation but degrade; mechanical valves need it, with the warfarin versus heparin dilemma.
- Postpartum: ICU or HDU monitoring for the autotransfusion.

### Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.


## Self-marking checklist
- Explains the physiology of pregnancy and labour in mitral stenosis
- Uses mWHO classification and identifies PH and stenosis as highest risk
- Explains individual delivery mode, specialist-centre planning and risk-based higher-care monitoring
- Aims for slow heart rate, sinus rhythm and slowly titrated epidural
- Avoids precipitants of raised PVR and sudden SVR drop
- Addresses anticoagulation and valve type
- Plans postpartum monitoring

**Audit evidence map:** BB23 rheumatic disease; preg25. Source depth and any limitations are recorded in the audit register.

items.title: 2023.1 Q6: Mechanical aortic valve through pregnancy and delivery
items.q: Discuss the implications of anticoagulation as well as an appropriate anticoagulant management strategy for a 25-year-old with a mechanical aortic valve for the duration of pregnancy, delivery and the postpartum period.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report emphasis:** 2023.1 report verified: continued valve protection until close to delivery, fetal teratogenic/haemorrhage risks, neuraxial implications and major bleeding were core requirements.

### The problem

A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation and pregnancy is hypercoagulable, with changing drug requirements (higher volume of distribution, increased renal clearance). Every option trades **maternal valve thrombosis, stroke and death** against **fetal harm and bleeding**. Care is by a pregnancy heart team (cardiology, obstetrics, anaesthesia, haematology) with the patient's informed choice.

### Agents and implications

| Agent | Maternal efficacy | Fetal and practical issues |
|---|---|---|
| **Warfarin** | Most effective | Crosses the placenta: teratogenic in the first trimester (embryopathy at weeks 6 to 12, lower risk if dose 5 mg/day or less), fetal intracranial haemorrhage, miscarriage |
| **LMWH** (twice daily) | Better fetal outcomes but more valve thrombosis than warfarin | Does not cross the placenta; needs anti-Xa monitoring (peak anti-Xa target individualised to valve/type/risk; ESC 2025 discusses 1.0–1.2 IU/mL) because weight-based dosing is inaccurate as fluid state changes |
| **UFH** (aPTT guided) | Effective but hard to keep in range | No placental transfer; used peripartum; HIT, osteoporosis |
| **DOACs** | Contraindicated (mechanical valve and pregnancy) | |

### Suggested strategy

- **First trimester:** after informed discussion, continue warfarin if dose is 5 mg/day or less (European and US guidance), otherwise twice-daily LMWH or UFH for the first trimester (the Australian rheumatic heart disease approach), then back to warfarin from about week 13. There is no consensus on the optimal regimen.
- **Second and third trimester:** warfarin (valve-specific INR (often target 2.5 for a bileaflet aortic valve without extra risk; higher for relevant valve/patient factors)) or LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring; echo surveillance. Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception, which adds thrombotic risk.
- **Before planned delivery:** switch VKA to adjusted heparin at least two weeks beforehand (often around 36 weeks), allowing fetal VKA clearance. For a mechanical valve, consider conversion from LMWH to IV UFH at least 36 h before planned delivery under the pregnancy-heart-team protocol; stop UFH 4–6 h before delivery/neuraxial intervention and confirm recovery.
- **Delivery:** agree timing and mode individually with the pregnancy heart team. Stop therapeutic LMWH at least 24 hours before neuraxial block or delivery (use IV UFH, stopped 4 to 6 hours before). If labour starts on warfarin, caesarean section is advised because of fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk.
- **Postpartum:** restart anticoagulation according to bleeding, valve risk and neuraxial timing; distinguish prophylactic from therapeutic dosing. Therapeutic LMWH usually waits ≥24 h after lower-risk surgery or 48–72 h after high-risk surgery; remove catheter ≥4 h before first dose and wait ≥24 h from needle placement. All are compatible with breastfeeding.

### Anaesthetic implications

- Neuraxial block needs normal coagulation (INR normalised to the local laboratory range for neuraxial insertion; catheter removal generally requires INR <1.5; 24 hours after therapeutic LMWH; UFH off with normal aPTT) and observance of catheter removal intervals. Alternatives are remifentanil PCA or general anaesthesia.
- Avoid tachycardia and hypotension (aortic valve disease); slow epidural top-ups; oxytocin by infusion.
- Anticoagulation raises the risk of peripartum haemorrhage, so prepare for postpartum haemorrhage with early surgical management, and for reversal (protamine for heparins, vitamin K and PCC for warfarin). General anaesthesia is needed for caesarean section if anticoagulation cannot be stopped.
- **Suspected valve thrombosis** (new dyspnoea, embolism or altered click) needs urgent imaging and pregnancy-heart-team treatment. Anticoagulation, thrombolysis or surgery depend on obstruction, stability, valve and gestation; none is automatic.

Gives a staged plan including the switch at about 36 weeks
Explains delivery planning and caesarean if on warfarin in labour
Explains neuraxial implications and intervals, and alternatives

items.title: How should delivery be planned in rheumatic heart disease?
items.q: How should delivery be planned in rheumatic heart disease?
items.a:
- Vaginal delivery preferred if no obstetric indication.
- mWHO II: spontaneous labour if close to hospital.
- mWHO III or IV: planned delivery in an expert centre with appropriate monitoring, sometimes ICU depending on severity; not obligatory ICU induction for every mWHO III/IV patient.
- Planned caesarean can suit the highest-risk patients.

> **Closing point:** Plan timing, people and place before labour starts.

Source: Blue Book 2023

items.title: 3. Peripartum cardiomyopathy
items.q: A woman presents 2 weeks postpartum with breathlessness and orthopnoea and is found to have LV systolic dysfunction. Discuss peripartum cardiomyopathy and the anaesthetic considerations for a future delivery.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Anaesthesia and peripartum cardiomyopathy" (BJA Educ 2023).

### Definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an **idiopathic cardiomyopathy causing heart failure from LV systolic dysfunction** (EF nearly always below 45%) **towards the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery**, with no other cause. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and occurs in previously healthy women. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of pregnancy-related death in high-income countries.

### Recognition

Symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea) overlap with normal pregnancy, so diagnosis is delayed. **Measure BNP** in women with orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, then ECG and echo.

### Preop

### Management

- Specialist-centre, **multidisciplinary pregnancy heart team** including the anaesthetist.
- Heart failure treatment adjusted for pregnancy or lactation: diuretics, beta-blocker, vasodilators (hydralazine and nitrate while pregnant; ACE inhibitors after delivery).
- Anticoagulation if EF is very low because of thrombus risk.
- Advanced support (ECLS, VAD) in refractory cases.

### Delivery

- **Vaginal delivery with neuraxial analgesia** where possible. Early, slowly titrated epidural reduces pain, tachycardia and preload and afterload swings.
- Caesarean for obstetric indication or haemodynamic instability; titrated epidural or CSE, or general anaesthesia with invasive monitoring.
- Invasive arterial monitoring in unstable patients; avoid fluid overload; oxytocin by slow infusion.
- Postpartum HDU or ICU.

### Prognosis

Recovery of EF is common, but women are at **increased risk of recurrent heart failure in later pregnancies**, and counselling is needed.

### Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.


## Self-marking checklist
- Defines PPCM with timing, EF below 45% and exclusion of other causes
- Recommends BNP, ECG and echo for suggestive symptoms
- Uses a multidisciplinary heart team
- Prefers vaginal delivery with neuraxial analgesia
- Plans titrated neuraxial or general anaesthesia for caesarean with monitoring
- Notes recurrence risk and need for counselling

**Audit evidence map:** BJAEd PPCM 2023; preg25. Source depth and any limitations are recorded in the audit register.
